title: Mix the two layers in a separatory funnel by shaking it
instruction: Mix the two layers in the separatory funnel by shaking it, then put it back in its support with the stopper in.
context: Liquid-liquid extraction in a separatory funnel is routine work in chemistry, pharmaceutical and environmental labs. Organic lab manuals and lab-safety guidance teach the same handling: hold the stopper in, turn the funnel over with the stem pointing up and away from people (into the back of the hood), open the stopcock at once to vent, then shake a few times and vent again, repeating as you mix. Unvented, solvent vapour or CO2 pressure blows the stopper out and sprays the contents; opening the stopcock with the stem down drains the lower layer. Only the goal is given: one arm turns the funnel over and shakes it, the other turns the stopcock key a quarter turn and back. Unlike #520 (shake a capped cocktail tin with both hands: no valve, no venting) and #374 (open a vent before draining a fixed tank: a one-off order step), the relief here is periodic, on a held vessel, with the outlet's direction controlled. Done by: chemical technicians; chemists (O*NET 19-4031.00, 19-2031.00).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward toward the back of the hood, y left). Funnel: a 120 g borosilicate glass separatory funnel standing upright, bulb centre at x 30, y 12, 15 cm above the table: an octagonal bulb 5.6 cm across and 6 cm tall, a 2.4 cm neck, a 2.4 cm taper and a 1 x 1 x 6 cm stem with a PTFE stopcock barrel 3.2 cm below the bulb. Stopcock key: a 5 g white PTFE key on a short shaft beside the stem (its 2.6 x 2 x 0.8 cm paddle 3.3-5.3 cm from the stem axis), turning a quarter turn about the plug axis (pointing 40 deg left of forward); shut across the stem, open in line with it; it stays where it is turned. Stopper: a 10 g ground-glass stopper on the neck. Support: two fixed rubber-coated steel rails 8 cm long, 4.4 cm apart, along the plug axis, their tops 12 cm above the table, on a grey steel post and base; the bulb rests on them, the stem and stopcock hang between them.
scoring: From the episode's recorded poses (the trial video on a real rig). A pressure counter: turning the funnel over (stem above horizontal) adds 2 once, each shaking stroke adds 1 (the bulb moving 3 cm or more between turning points while turned over with the stopcock under 20 deg), and opening the stopcock past 45 deg with the stem at least 30 deg above horizontal resets it to 0. Latched 0 for the rest of the trial: the counter reaching 6 (the stopper blows out), or the stopcock opened past 45 deg with the stem less than 30 deg above horizontal (liquid runs out). Otherwise 0.25 after 4 strokes, 0.5 after 8, and 1.0 after 8 with the funnel back in its support (bulb centre within 1 cm of its seat, within 5 mm of its height, tilt under 10 deg), the stopcock under 10 deg, the stopper in, funnel, key and stopper let go (both grippers 2.5 cm clear) and none of them moved more than 1 mm or 1 deg over the last control step, success when held 1 s. Capped at 0.5 if it was ever vented with the stem pointing back toward the arms. Scored at the last step. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: Stand the funnel back in its support with the stopcock shut and the stopper seated (re-bonded); on a real rig, refill the two layers (water under a coloured light oil) and reset the pressure counter, or use a funnel with a small sealed gas cartridge; the support does not move.
fidelity: Rigid boxes, one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). The vapour pressure is a counter, not gas: turning over +2, each 3 cm stroke +1, venting resets it; at 6 the stopper's hold is let go and it drops out. Liquid and its draining are not simulated (opening with the stem low is scored 0). The stopcock key is a hinge with Coulomb friction (0.01 N*m); the bulb is an octagon of boxes. The outcome is judged from simulator poses every step.
